title: Where We Work
body:
The Task Force operates in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, primarily in Gratiot County. The Pine River watershed originates west of Alma and St. Louis, Michigan, arcs northeast, and merges with the Chippewa and Tittabawassee rivers at Midland to form the Saginaw River, which empties into Saginaw Bay and Lake Huron.

The region sits atop brine deposits that attracted chemical manufacturers, and a small oil field once supported local refineries — the last of which, in Alma, was operated by Total Petroleum. St. Louis became home to Michigan Chemical Company, later Velsicol Chemical, whose disposal practices created three federal Superfund sites plus one state-regulated contaminated site. Combined with waste from other refineries and manufacturers, these operations made the Pine River one of the most polluted rivers in the country; Michigan has issued its highest-level health warnings against eating fish caught from it.

## Three focus communities

**St. Louis, Michigan** — Originally a Saginaw Chippewa settlement and later a German Lutheran mission town, incorporated in 1858. Once known for mineral spas, it became a chemical and refining center in the early 20th century. Velsicol's 1973 PBB contamination accident forced the plant's 1978 closure, devastating the local economy until state-built prisons reversed the population decline.

**Alma, Michigan** — Gratiot County's largest city (population 8,995 as of 2020) and its financial and healthcare hub, home to Alma College and several manufacturing facilities. The city hosted oil refineries until 1999; the Task Force continues to address extensive water table and river contamination left by the former Total Petroleum facility.

**Breckenridge, Michigan** — A town of roughly 1,300 residents centered on a bean and grain elevator. A non-Hodgkin's lymphoma cluster was identified here in 1974 — ten cases between 1954 and 1973, about twelve times the expected rate. Velsicol also buried low-level radioactive waste nearby, along Bush Creek.

## Superfund and contaminated sites

**Gratiot County Landfill** (MID 980506281) — A 40-acre site southeast of St. Louis, licensed in 1974 for domestic, commercial, and industrial waste disposal. It contains roughly 269,000 pounds of PBBs and required cleanup with ongoing maintenance.

**Smith Farm** — A wooded, partly swampy area south of St. Louis where several local companies, including Velsicol, disposed of waste. In 1990 the EPA ordered Velsicol to remove hundreds of drums of hazardous material.

**Velsicol Burn Pit** (MID 98079431) — A 5-acre site west of the main plant where Michigan Chemical/Velsicol burned industrial waste and pesticides between 1956 and 1970. Velsicol claimed to have removed contaminated soil in 1983, but the EPA later found large-scale contamination remained and placed the site on the National Priorities List in 2010.

**Velsicol Chemical Corp. Site** (MID 000722439) — The 54-acre former plant in St. Louis, operating since 1936 for pesticide production and shut down in 1977. Investigations found pesticides in soil and groundwater; the contamination footprint expanded to nine city blocks and a 30-mile downriver floodplain, and a fish consumption advisory remains in effect.

**Breckenridge Low-Level Radioactive Waste Site** — Located six miles east of St. Louis near Bush Creek, this site received low-level radioactive waste from rare-earth production in the 1960s. Cleanup occurred under a Fruit of the Loom bankruptcy settlement in 2002.

## Beyond the watershed

The 1973 PBB food contamination accident affected people well beyond the watershed itself, since it entered Michigan's food supply. The Task Force welcomes international participation and has engaged with the International Joint Commission (the U.S.–Canada Great Lakes agency) and international health experts.
